summary: Eolo was an Italian boy whom Harold Mellor's household acquired by purchase - 200 lire, paid to his father - and who was with Mellor on the Riviera in 1898-99 and in Paris in September 1900. Wilde met him when the two bicycled over to Napoule, recorded the purchase, recorded that Mellor was bored by him, and twenty months later described him as Mellor's 'slave, who like all slaves is most tyrannical'.

sources.quote: Sometimes a very pretty, slim, fair-haired Italian boy bicycles over with him. His name is Eolo; his father, who sold him to Harold for 200 lire, having christened all his children – seventeen in number – out of the Mythological Dictionary. Harold is a nice fellow, but his boy bores him. It is dreadfully sad.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 2 January 1899, Napoule - immediately after the sentences on Mellor's Harrow expulsion and daily bicycle visits. 'Eolo' and 'Mythological Dictionary' are italicised in the original.
sources.supports: What the correspondence records of Eolo's position in Mellor's household: the purchase from his father for 200 lire, his name, and Mellor's boredom with him
sources.provenance: PDF page 1162, printed folio 1116 confirmed on rendered page. Contiguous run from a page; no elision inside this quote.

sources.quote: He is now in Paris with his slave Eolo, who like all slaves is most tyrannical.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Saturday, 1 September [1900], Paris, reporting on Mellor after the 'Mellor cure' at Gland; the next sentence begins 'He and I, however, are great' and completes on printed 1195 with 'friends.'
sources.supports: The same relation twenty months later, in Wilde's plain word - Eolo still described as Mellor's property
sources.provenance: PDF page 1240, printed folio 1194 confirmed on rendered page.
